idiom_name: explicit snapshot struct with a deep-copied payload, history as a hand-managed array
implementation_notes: C has no language-level deep copy and cannot hide a struct's members from other translation units, so the classic structure must be written by hand and the narrow interface becomes a header convention: forward-declare the snapshot type in the header, define it in one .c file, and hand the caretaker only `const struct memento *` values it can store and free. Copy value members with struct assignment or memcpy, but copy every owned pointer explicitly (malloc plus memcpy/strdup) - a struct assignment alone duplicates the pointers, not the storage behind them. A fixed-size ring buffer or a dynamically grown array of snapshots is the caretaker, and restore copies the payload back into the originator and re-establishes its invariants. The effort is justified where undo is a real requirement (editors, embedded UIs, protocol state machines, audio/game state); for a one-shot cancel there is no simpler form than not mutating a committed copy.
pitfalls: Struct assignment and memcpy copy pointer members verbatim, so the 'snapshot' keeps aliasing the live buffer and a later edit rewrites history - deep-copy every owned allocation and record its length or sentinel.
memcpy with overlapping source and destination is undefined behaviour (the glibc 2.13 episode showed how late that bug surfaces); use memmove whenever the ranges can overlap.

Ownership errors are the typical failure: snapshots leaked on early error paths, double-freed when the history is trimmed, or dangling because the originator freed a buffer the snapshot still references.
A memento from another originator instance is type-compatible but semantically wrong; tag snapshots with their owner or document that restore is instance-specific.
